utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T, The Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Alexis Demirdjian and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if there are no housekeeping --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just one, Your Honours, and that is the question of scanning the diary, so that it's quite clear. We've spoken to the evidence unit, it's going to take, because of staffing problems, a couple of days to do it so what we propose to do, we've brought them back for the witness and at the end of each day we'll take them away and try and get them scanned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'm resisting the opportunity to say -- to make any comment on the fact that the OTP is experiencing staffing problems. Could the usher please -- I see he has gone to escort the witness. Ms. Korner, perhaps you could repeat in the hearing of the witness when he comes the delay -- reason for the delay in getting the documents back to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But without the staffing problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, to you, sir. Before I invite Ms. Korner to resume her cross examination, I remind you you are still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, we'll give Mr. Bjelosevic his original notebooks back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, can I explain, we wanted to copy them properly but it's going to take a little time. So what we are going to ask you to do is at the end of each day, if you leave them with us so they can be copied. It will take about two days. I see you shrugging, but you agree with that, you are happy?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just one final the matter, the documents that you brought with you yesterday which you hadn't provide copies of before, leaving aside the CDs, are those statements taken by Inspector Solaja about the incident involving the Mice in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because it wasn't entirely clear exactly what they were. I want to go back, please, then to where we left off yesterday, namely discussing membership of the SDS. You told us in interview, and I believe in court as well, that although you would be a member of the communist party, you had not joined one of the nationalist parties which sprung up in -- for the purpose of the 1990 elections; that's correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You equally told us that you were sympathetic to the aims of the SDS which was to remain in the former Yugoslavia. However, at the time the SDS was founded, that wasn't a consideration, was it, because at that stage, nobody was suggesting the split of the various republics?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their programme was defined from the very point of the foundation of the party and their aims were publicised and that was already a time when there was talk about the so-called disassociation of Yugoslavia, and on the top of that list was Slovenia. These programme aims were from the very beginning placed in the public domain.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: After you became the head of the CSB Doboj in about May of 1991 was there at least one occasion when Radovan Karadzic visited Doboj?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please switch off the mike while the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure, believe me. It is possible but I don't remember any such event.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: An occasion when you -- an occasion when you and Mr. Ninkovic, who was the head of the SDS, were seen together with Mr. Karadzic, did that ever happen?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Had you ever met Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but never with Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where and -- firstly, how often have you met Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In person?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In person.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could hardly remember after such a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you have a pretty clear memory of most things, Mr. Bjelosevic, as we've already seen. Surely you remember how often you met the president of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to be in the same locations where the president of the Republika Srpska was, those were different locations. However, how many times that took place, I honestly cannot remember. What you mentioned a minute ago about the meeting with Ninkovic and myself, I know that that didn't happen because otherwise I would have remembered. President Karadzic used to come to Brod. He sometimes came to Derventa as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Therefore, we had certain obligations in order to provide security details and things like that, but I can really not remember on how many occasions that took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me ask you about some things --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I leave it on, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, please, sir, about some things that were said about you and see whether you can assist us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have a look, please, at the document which is -- its 65 ter number is 20000 and it's tab 2 of our documents. You haven't got a binder, Mr. Bjelosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is an intercept of a conversation between Mr. Karadzic and Branko Ostojic. Did you know Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know him personally, but if I'm not mistaken, he was in the government. However, I don't know which position he held.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll come back to this in a minute. It's on the 23rd of July of 1991, and Mr. Ostojic is speaking to Karadzic, you can see, it's not altogether clear who, but asked about that guy, and you said: "Doboj and Banja Luka and Gorazde." And Karadzic said: "Yes." Branko Ostojic says: "Is there someone in Doboj, a name of a person he could call?" And Mr. Karadzic says: "Andrija Bjelosevic."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we go, please, to the next page in both B/C/S and English. I think it's the bottom of the B/C/S, sorry, could we go back to the first page. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Karadzic says: "Yes, because they have a procedure for everything to go through...," whatever it means, "all right." Karadzic says: "Just get and Andrija." Ostojic says: "He is a good man." Karadzic: "Excellent, we need a professional."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: "He's a real one." Karadzic: "We need a professional and he is 100 per cent professional." Now, this is July, a couple of months after you've been appointed as CSB Doboj. Do you have any idea on what basis Mr. Karadzic is calling you Andrija and saying what an excellent fellow you are?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see here, it is Ostojic who is referring to someone as a proper guy or the right guy. And, yes, he did ask Karadzic who can this guy report to, if I understand properly, but if I were to find any logic in this, since there is mention also here of this guy being the right one and a true professional and then President Karadzic says, Yes, excellent, we do need professionals. So if I were to put this picture together, that probably referred to someone to be admitted into service or somewhere else. If I'm not wrong in drawing these kind of conclusions because this is the first time I've seen this document and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think you misunderstood the question. You can't remember how many times you met Karadzic but he is calling you Andrija in July of 1991, and says that you are a professional --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, Your Honours, I don't understand where Ms. Korner finds this reference to calling -- Karadzic calling the witness professional. This is a complete misinterpretation of the document and the witness explained what the document says. I don't see -- I've been trying to find out in the English translation, but the English translation appears to be genuine, but it's obvious that it's referred to another person.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I am sorry, this is a matter of comment and an improper one, I may say, Mr. Zecevic. But my reading of it is that Mr. Karadzic says: "Just get Andrija." Ostojic says: "He's a good man." Karadzic: "Excellent, we need a professional." Ostojic: "He's a real one." Now ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, you have to read the whole document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I've read the whole document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I don't want to waste time on unnecessary argument. We've got enough to get through as it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Explain to me, would you please, Mr. Bjelosevic, how it is that Karadzic in July of 1991 is calling you Andrija?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For God sake, that's my name. I don't see anything here. That's my name and I really don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but if he didn't know you at all in 1991 in July, wouldn't he be calling you Andrija Bjelosevic in full or Bjelosevic or Mr. Bjelosevic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see here there's my full name mentioned twice and then further down below there's only my first name. I am not saying that Mr. Karadzic didn't know the people on the ground who were discharging some important duties, and I believe that the head of CSB is an important position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Between -- well, by July of 1991, shortly after you had been appointed to Doboj CSB, did you know and had you -- sorry, had you met Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In person?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In person.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer. The interpreters couldn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that by that time I had an opportunity to meet Karadzic in person. Of course, I knew who he was and what he was doing and things of that nature, but, if I remember correctly, there was no meeting in person by that time with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Had you spoken to him on the telephone?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke with him on the telephone, but I cannot remember at this moment when that happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And why were you speaking to Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, the first time, I think, had to do with my appointment to the position of the head of the Security Services Centre because Mr. Ninkovic reacted very overwhelmingly from the very beginning, and I postponed, or rather, I did not accept to proceed with a hand-over with the previous head Nikolic knowing what it means if you don't have the approval of the political circles and that could create problems. Then, maybe two days later, I received a call from Mr. Karadzic from the office of the political party, that he told me that I should ignore the opinion of the local politicians and that I should accept what had been ordered by the MUP to be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's the situation, isn't it, that went throughout 1991, that unfortunately, presumably for a professional police officer, politics, nationalist politics had entered into the MUP; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please switch off the mike.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand this correctly, whether it's a bad translation or whether it's some confusion between nationalism and national politics. Could you please be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, from what you've told us about having to ring Mr. Karadzic about your appointment which should have been entirely an internal MUP matter, you are describing, are you not, a situation which prevailed through 1991, namely that politics, and by politics, I mean nationalist politics, had entered into the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only wrong statement is that it was me who called Mr. Karadzic. I didn't call him. It was the other way around. I received a call and that was a very prominent feature when it had to do with the personnel of all ethnic groups. The local politicians had their respective favourite and that applied to the personnel from all the three communities, the Serbs, the Muslim and the Croat. And maybe it would be advisable if we clarified this in more detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, Mr. Bjelosevic, I really have a lot to get through. I accept entirely that it's not only the SDS, it is the HDZ and the SDA who also are bringing politics into the MUP. Now, unless you really feel that something else needs to be said, can we move on because I do have a lot to get through.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really think that we should do this for the sake of clarity. I said earlier that Milan Ninkovic was the preferred candidate. However, since this had not been endorsed by the MUP, Mr. Ninkovic and the people around him were dissatisfied from the very beginning and they reacted against me which prompted me to call Mr. Zepinic because I had known him from before, and I told him that there was a problem and that Mr. Ninkovic was the preferred candidate. Mr. Zepinic said also that I should take no notice of that, that I should assume my duties and that as far as the political problems were concerned, he was going to have certain talks within certain circles and that after that I should report to my duty station. After that, I presume that Mr. Zepinic contacted Mr. Karadzic which was followed by the call from Mr. Karadzic because that is when I was told that I should assume my position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I want to move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have a look, please, now at the next document which is tab 3, please. Sorry, it's 65 ter 2001. 20001.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is roughly two and a half weeks later. This is an intercept of a conversation between Karadzic and a man called Neso, whoever that may be. And Neso, at the bottom of the page in English, says: "What I wanted to say to you was, I said, I should send somebody to Doboj, this Bjelosevic. He says he has some news for you." Karadzic says: "Bjelosevic?"

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go to the second page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then Neso says: "Yes, to send somebody in the morning by car to his place," he says, "you can't possibly like it this." And Karadzic says: "He can't come, can he." Neso says: "He can't. Somebody," he says, "should come over to him ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we need to go to the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And there's a conversation about a man called Micevic. And then Karadzic at the bottom says: "We'll see." And Neso says: "He tells me it's very important and to pass it on to you." First of all, do you know who this man Neso is?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm trying to put this all together into a logical whole. This is the first time I see this. I cannot understand who Neso might be and what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, can you think of any reason why in August of 1991, why you so urgently needed to give some news to Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea what this might be, and I do not remember that I sent any kind of information in that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Bjelosevic, were you close to the political leadership of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you saw from that document what my standing with them was like. I was under permanent pressure, and I think that this culminated sometime in December 1992 when at the meeting of the Municipal Assembly a few members of the Municipal Assembly had been prepared in a way to degrade my work and my position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the Doboj SDS, Mr. Bjelosevic, I'm talking about the leadership at the top of the party, that is to say, Karadzic, Stojic, Plavsic, Zepinic at that stage?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have known Mr. Zepinic since before the war. As for the other people you mentioned from the leadership, I absolutely had no, how should I put this, close contacts or any special contacts except when somebody would call me. I just remembered that sometime in the summer of 1991 Mr. Koljevic called me as well. Perhaps that could be linked to that telephone conversation, but I truly cannot remember who Neso is. The name doesn't ring a bell at all. Mr. Koljevic called me, the late Mr. Koljevic called me, in relation to what had happened in Slavonski Brod. If you allow me, perhaps I could explain that, perhaps that has something to do with it. I'm really doing my best to find some logic, some connection, but I am not sure that that is it. In Slavonski Brod --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, this is August 1991 so that has got nothing to do with what happened in Slavonski Brod, has it? This conversation?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I'm trying to see what this might be linked to. And what crossed my mind just now is what happened in Slavonski Brod in the summer of 1991. That is when I received a call in relation to what had happened. It was the late Koljevic who called me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps that was it. But I cannot remember who Neso is and who that might be. I really don't know. However, I remember this event and I know that there were a few calls in relation to that, but the first person to call me about this was the late Mr. Koljevic. He called and asked me about what had happened in the settlement of Bjelis. That is a settlement that came into being when the population from the right bank of the Sava river moved into Slavonski Brod in order to be protected from floods and that is when that settlement had been blocked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then all of these people were arrested, brought into custody, and I was asked whether I could find out what this was all about. I went to Bosanski Brod then and I spoke to Chief Pranjic, and I went with him to Slavonski Brod as well to see Mr. Dedic, the chief of the police administration. Perhaps that is what this was all about. I don't know what else it could have been though. At that point in time, we did have some talks there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I simply am asking you, and you can say yes or no, Mr. Bjelosevic, whether or not you were -- and whether or not you were a member of the SDS, you were close to the political leadership of the SDS at the top level?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off. We cannot hear the witness. We did not hear the beginning of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ... by the members of the Presidency of the BH. I remember that Koljevic contacted me. I remember that once or twice Mrs. Plavsic contacted me as well, if I remember correctly, but as members of the BH Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you cannot remember how many times --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, Ms. Korner, the interpreter's note says that the first part of the answer was not important, and I think it's important because he gave the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Amazing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm told the first part of your answer wasn't interpreted. Could you tell us, please, what you said. My question was, let me repeat it, and it can be answered in one sentence, Mr. Bjelosevic, believe me: Were you close to the political leadership of the SDS at the top level?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, one further question on this business of your contacts with the top.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look, please, at document P198 which is tab 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. These are the minutes of -- it seems to be a stenographic record, but there's two separate documents, but this is the one I want you to look at the for the moment, of the Assembly of the Serbian people on the 24th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go, please, to page 4 in English and page 5, I think, in B/C/S -- no, page 4 in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the election of the members of the government of the Serbian Republic. And we need to go to the next page in both B/C/S and English. This is where Djeric proposes Mico Stanisic of the minister of foreign affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then could we go to the next page in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is a document you've seen before, isn't it, Mr. Bjelosevic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really haven't seen it until now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was shown to you, wasn't it, in interview in 2004 by Mr. Sebire?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your answer wasn't recorded. I don't know why this is, but there's a real difficulty in the mike picking up your voice, I don't know whether they can be adjusted. Could you repeat your answer, please, Mr. Bjelosevic.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall having seen this before, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'm going to take you to the bit in the interview at the moment. Mr. Djuric, whoever he may be, suggests: "On behalf of the Municipal Board of the SDS, I would like to suggest a candidate who does not come from Prnjavor, but from Doboj. I refer to Mr. Andrija Bjelosevic, a very competent and honourable man." Jovo Mijatovic, I assume you know who he was: "Considering the present state of affairs in the MUP, it would be a good idea if the candidate addressed the Assembly and said a few words about it." Now, do you know who Mr. Djuric was?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, he was an MP from Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was he somebody that you had friendly relationship with?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we just knew each other. I just knew who the man was. We did not have any kind of a personal or friendly relationship.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we then go, please, to page 9 in English. Mico Stanisic then makes a speech which I don't think we need trouble you with. Page 9 in English and 8 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Srdjo Srdic says: "I am a very close and good friend of Mr. Bjelosevic. I do not understand, however, why we should start to discuss new suggestions ...," et cetera. Who is Mr. Srdic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Srdic was an MP from Prijedor. I don't know since it's only the last name that is involved, maybe it refers to the late Milovan Bjelosevic, he was no friend of mine, and I just note that he was an MP. I don't think that this had to do with me, what it says here, that he is a great friend of Bjelosevic's because we were not friends. I just knew Mr. Srdic as an MP. He was considerably older than myself and I really don't think that this has anything to do with me, if you thought that it was about me. May I just comment upon Mr. Djuric's proposal, too. I'm honoured by that kind of praise. And you saw that in that letter and decision of the regional SDS board that they also say that they are not challenging my professional or moral qualities but that I'm not their representative.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, going back to the reference by Mr. Srdic, who was, in fact, not only assembly man but the leader, was he not, of the SDS in Prijedor? That's right, isn't it, until he was replaced by, forgot the man's name now.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about him being in the top echelons of the SDS. I just know him as an MP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Replaced by Mr. Miskovic, I think it was. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But going back just very brief to this quote because I don't want it to get too buried in it, it's clearly referring to you isn't it. Because it says: "I'm a close and very good friend of Mr. Bjelosevic. I do not understand, however, why we should start to discuss new suggestions when the matter falls in the competence of the prime minister designate." And this is all about the suggestion that -- of who should be minister of internal affairs. So do you accept he is clearly referring to you and not to your cousin?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not agree with you because this seems to me to be a response to what somebody else had said during the debate. I'm really not familiar with the details, but it is possible that the late Milovan Bjelosevic said something when he took part in the debate. Perhaps he relied on Djuric's proposal. Because how could he mention me as an excellent friend of his when that was absolutely not the case? As for Mr. Srdic, in person, I may have seen him only three or four times in my life. However, I did see him on television when sessions of parliament were telecast and he often took part in the debate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I don't propose to pursue this any further. I want to look next, please, with you, Mr. Bjelosevic, at the events, some of the major events which -- about which you've said nothing during the course of your testimony to -- when Mr. Zecevic was asking you questions, which surrounded the break-up in the MUP. Now, you talked a lot about what you called the parallel structure that was being set up by the SDA or the HDZ within the Socialist Federal Republic MUP. For example, at page 19451. In fact, this was in answer to a question from Judge Harhoff, and this was to do with the Bosanski Brod-Slavonski Brod discussions: "At the time, there existed a certain amount of co-ordination, and there were plans between certain people in the Bosanski Brod police station and the police administration in Slavonski Brod; that is to say, there was a parallel structure." And then later, you were talking about, at page 19455: "Stations establishing direct communication with the personnel administration and some of the chiefs and pointed in violation of some of the regulations, and gradually it all gained the hallmarks of a shadow parallel system which caused the whole entire system to be undermined." And there were other quotes as well. You were aware, weren't you, however, that the SDS was also planning its own parallel system within the MUP? The MUP, certainly by the end of 1991, was already beginning to be divided, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you quoted is something I explained sufficiently when I spoke at the time and I supported it with documents. You will see from these remarks made by Prkacin on television that he confirms that. As for the break-up of the MUP that you referred to just now, I don't know where you see the Serbian side doing something parallel in 1991. I did not see any such thing, at least not in the area where I was chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let me show you one more intercept, please, which is P897 and it's at tab 2A.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That is conversation between Mr. Zepinic and Karadzic in July of 1991. In fact, the day after there's a conversation that we showed you -- I showed you that refers to you. It's a very long conversation and it relates to appointments in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go, please, in the English page 9; and in the B/C/S page 6, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In anticipation what Ms. Korner intends to do, I object because I don't see the basis that she can pose the question to this witness showing him a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Let's have a question, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but -- well, I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said that you had no evidence that the SDS was planning a parallel structure at the same time, and, indeed, we would suggest earlier than -- there was any suggestion of this by the SDA or the HDZ. Now, appreciating that you haven't seen this particular intercept before, do you see in the middle of the page Karadzic saying: "Please let the collegium meet every morning and clear all that out. I was with Izetbegovic last night and with Zulfikarpasic, and I told him right into his face, we'll establish a parallel government, parallel police, we'll withdraw our people and they'd have to be paid by the government. We'll withdraw all our people under arms. We'll establish an entire parallel state, if you keep on screwing us." Now, you knew, didn't you, because, I suggest, of your contacts with the leadership that this was happening, that already the SDS was saying, We are going to set up a parallel police? Mr. Zepinic, your friend, didn't he tell you about this?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is really the first time that I see this. And I would like to say once again in the area where I was chief, in those municipalities at that time no parallel system had been established by the Serbs who were in the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that area, as far as I know, and I think that I had a good overview of the situation and that I was following all the developments, I had no information in that regard. And this is the first time that I see these particular minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, no, no, can I say and make it clear entirely, I'm not suggesting that you have ever seen the record of this conversation before. What I'm asking you is whether your good friend Mr. Zepinic, who you knew, you told us, did not explain to you what was going on between Karadzic, the SDA, the SDS and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we never spoke about this subject, but if you would permit me to explain my relationship with Zepinic, we knew each other before the war because of the sports. I complained to him about certain things that were mentioned in my earlier testimony, and it is my opinion that there was never a serious reaction to my complaints, an effort to change something. I spoke to him and complained to him about the problems that I had encountered in my area. So his role and his power was undefined, if you ask me. Whenever I complained to him about the problems that I had encountered, the fact that didn't have enough materiel, vehicle, and other things, he would always assure me that Mr. Delimustafic was a good man and the two of them were going to see to it, while actually nothing happened. And we had very little materiel compared to other areas, compared to other centres. Whatever help arrived went strait to the local stations. And I would like to repeat it once again that Zepinic never spoke to me about this subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just for the record, Mr. Bjelosevic, in your interview in 2004 going back to the Assembly document I showed you, you were shown that at page 10 of 14, and you said exactly then what you said today, namely, I saw this document for the first time. And, in fact, you, at that stage, said, I don't know which Djuric this is. Now, can we move on, please, through the major events, as I say, which you didn't touch upon during your earlier evidence. You no doubt recall on the 17th of October of 1991, the walkout by the SDS from the Assembly and the subsequent declaration of sovereignty that was made, if you can put it that way, but the Rump Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that event.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I want you to look at a document that's dated two days later, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which is tab 6A. Sorry, the 65 ter number -- sorry, Your Honours, I forgot to update my own document. It's, Your Honours -- I'm so sorry. It's P521.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm told it's 6B. For some reason I put it in 6A but it's 6B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: For a very good reason, Ms. Korner, because there is no 6A.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, what happened was I selected it then thought it will be 6A because of the date, and obviously for some reason we missed out A.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is a document, as I say, two days after the walkout, which is headed: "Possibilities of Organising a Serbian Ministry of the Interior."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we go, please, to the second page in B/C/S and it's the third page in English, please. There's a paragraph that begins -- second paragraph in English, and it's the -- sorry, we need the third page in B/C/S as well. I am sorry:

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "The minister of the interior, as an official in charge of the MUP, is legally entitled to issue orders, direct the work of, and assert control over, the administrations at the MUP headquarters, the CSB, Sarajevo SUP, and the public security stations. He is the only person authorised by the law to hire staff, assign them to posts, transfer and suspend them, conduct disciplinary procedures against them...," and so on, "he may, however, transfer elements of his authority to other employees."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry. Your Honours, I have to object. I think Ms. Korner should establish, first of all, with the witness whether he saw the document, does he know anything about the document, and then read from the document because this is just reading for the purposes of record, I think, and not for posing a question. I don't see how. How can that be a basis for a question if the first part, like I said, wasn't established first?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If Mr. Zecevic waits, he will hear what my question is when I finish reading the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And, I, myself, don't see any harm insofar as it may be the more efficient way of directing the witness's attention to the particular portion in respect of which -- out of which a question would be framed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I won't go on reading because you've had a chance to read it yourself. Do you agree, Mr. Bjelosevic, with that summary of the authority and duties of the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not up to me to agree or disagree with the rights and duties of the minister are stipulated by law, the Law on the Government and the Law on the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, you've been a policemen in the Republika Srpska and the previous administration since 1991. Would you agree that is a correct summary of the minister's authority and powers?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe you misspoke. You said the Ministry of Republika Srpska in 1991, if I heard you correctly, maybe it was a mistake. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just don't try and avoid the question, please, Mr. Bjelosevic. Answer the question.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not trying to avoid anything, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As an experienced police officer now, do you agree that that is an accurate summary of the authority and the powers of the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As stipulated by law. That's about it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll ask it one more time: As an experienced police officer knowing the law, is that an accurate summary of the powers and the authority of the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The witness's answer was recorded, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm asking him for his own knowledge. I don't want him to say what the law is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that an accurate -- is that an accurate summary from his own knowledge and experience?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, the answer as at line 21, isn't that a clear answer to the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, as stipulated by -- I don't know what line 21. I've got.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Line 22: "As stipulated by law. That's about it, yes."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I make that line 11 on this -- I see. The computer is playing up slightly differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I interpret it as he agrees with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's right, it may just be me ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, the next part says, "Given the above organisation of the MUP," and he dealt with -- the author of this paper which is not clear, I dealt with it earlier: "The establishment of a Serbian MUP as a parallel organ of authority is possible in a number of ways." And he sets out those ways. Now, Mr. Bjelosevic, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: However, were you aware because of your position as the head of the CSB that because of what had happened on the 15th of October there was active discussion going on in the SDS about setting up a separate Serbian MUP, a parallel structure?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, there was a discussion about the Assembly of the Serbian people and the establishment of the minister council. As for the establishment of the Serbian MUP, I do not know that there were any activities in that direction at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were one of, I think, five CSBs, because at that stage there were nine, headed by a Serb, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the number of Serbian personnel, but, yes, it is correct that I was in Doboj. In Banja Luka, there was Mr. Zupljanin. I can't remember others. If it's really important, maybe I can --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll come to which ones they were in a later document. So you were never privy in October 1991 to any discussions about a parallel MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Microphone off, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember. I think that I had no knowledge about anything like that at the time. I know that there was some talk about the Assembly. That was the time when the declaration on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina was about to be proclaimed, and I know that there was quite a lively discussion at the Assembly about that topic. I also know that after that it was concluded that the Assembly of the Serbian people had to be established as well as the council of ministers. I also know that there was some talk about the referendum, about remaining in Yugoslavia. I remember that at the time it was a very, very live political activity related to these topics. As for the organising of a parallel MUP in that period, I really do not remember that there was anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You see, because the Assembly, as you rightly said, the first Assembly met a few days later, about a week later, on the 24th of October. Now, in your evidence to Mr. Zecevic, you were shown a letter dated the 24th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And for that, we need the Defence documents, tab 2, and I am afraid I have not the faintest idea -- tab 7. I have not the faintest idea what the number is. 764D1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's 1D439.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before we get into the detail of this and the point I want to make about it, this is one of the documents you allegedly -- you provided to the Defence of Mr. Stanisic. It is on the list number 73, I believe, 764D1. You didn't give any indication of where you got this letter from. In other words, was it a copy that you kept yourself, is it something that you copied from the archives; are you able to assist?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am afraid I can't remember with any certainty, but I remember this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. You had been describing all the abuses, as you put them, to Mr. Zecevic that had been going on about staffing and the like. And when you were asked about it at page 19459, you said, "This is precisely my" -- you were asked for your comments: "This is precisely my response to the violation of regulations and procedures where change in personnel was concerned. That's precisely what we were discussing a moment ago. These are the issues that undermined the very system of work." Is it a sheer coincidence that the very first letter of complaint that you wrote to the minister, Mr. Delimustafic, is dated the 24th of October, the day of the first Serbian Assembly and about a week after this document that we've just been looking at was produced.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is probably just a coincidence. It has absolutely nothing to do with the political events in Sarajevo. As you can see here, in this letter I listed specific examples, what happened and where it happened, when things were -- when activities were going on which were contrary to the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why had you waited until the 24th of October to write this complaint which deals with a number of different incidents?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe if it was dated on another day you would ask me why this other day. I really don't know. By then it was far too obvious that some things were going on contrary to the law and the regulations. There were some telephone warnings, and, after that, I thought that there should be some written trace, some written warning about the fact that some things were going on which were not supposed to be going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But if you considered this was so important why hadn't you written earlier letters to the minister saying, Look, there are all -- for example, that you appointed a chief to the Derventa SJB who doesn't meet the requirements? Immediately that happened, why didn't you write the letter or get in touch with the minister or Mr. Zepinic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that I complained by telephone on a number of occasions, but if you really want me to explain what exactly was my intention in writing this document, you can see that in the last paragraph. If I had some other ideas, I wouldn't have written the last paragraph where I say I propose that a working meeting should be held with the chiefs of CSB, wherein a friendly atmosphere should be discussed in with all the colleagues, and so on and so forth. So if I had some other intentions, I probably wouldn't have written this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Wasn't this all, Mr. Bjelosevic, setting up the reasons why you could legitimately say there has to be a -- or try and say legitimately there has to be a separate MUP? That you had no -- I put it to you squarely, Mr. Bjelosevic, you had no real intention of trying to cure the problems through the MUP as it then existed?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is something that you claim and you have the right to claim whatever you want. As for me, I'm telling you once again, on the full responsibility and quite honestly, at that time I knew nothing about the activities that you showed me a moment ago mentioned in the minutes you showed me. And my ultimate and very serious intention was to stop the unlawful activities and to have the MUP act in a way stipulated by law and other regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to move on to another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the first break for the morning and return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I ask, it may be just me but it seems incredibly hot in here, whether the air conditioning could be turned up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, I want to move on through the events towards the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have up, please, on the screen the document which is P1353.19, tab 7A.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the document which proclaims the Serb autonomous region of Northern Bosnia as an inseparable part of the state of Yugoslavia, and it's dated the 4th of November -- or, it states that the decision was made on the 4th of November, 1991. I take it, Mr. Bjelosevic, you were aware of the Serb autonomous regions?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I take it equally that you were aware of the founding or the declaration of Northern Bosnia Serb autonomous region?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, only this never came into being, nor were any organs constituted at this level. However, I am aware of this decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: May I say straightaway, Mr. Bjelosevic, I don't disagree with you on this. That unlike the Krajina, nothing much happened after the declaration and there certainly was no Crisis Staff, was there, of the autonomous region of Northern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was not a single organ there. This was a purely political decision and it never became operational, nothing materialised.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. There was, however --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, we can look at the next document on this, please. If we look at, please, P1353.18, which is at 7B.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There was, in fact, the day of the declaration a founding Assembly session, wasn't there? We can see that nominated to the -- not sure to the chair means exactly, but Blagoje Simic, he was from Bosanski Samac, wasn't he, leader of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your cousin Milovan Bjelosevic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was an MP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. And other people, I don't think we need worry too much about them. And Mr. Nikola Perisic, who -- if we go over to the third page in English and the second in B/C/S, we'll see that Mr. Perisic was elected to the position of president and Mr. Bjelosevic was elected vice-president. And you were aware of that, were you not?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of the Assembly. However, I don't see page 2 on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It should be, I hope. Is it the under 2E?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said, 2E. Do you see it there?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it would not be right to suggest, would it, Mr. Bjelosevic, that your appointment into the head of the CSB had anything to do with the SAO Northern Bosnia because, as you say, it never really operated?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Security Services Centre of Doboj, as well as the others, as far as I know, had been established on a territorial principle much earlier before all these events took place, and, as I understand it now and I did so at the time, implies political moves made by those who were in favour of the preservation of Yugoslavia, as well as the moves of those who were in favour of disintegration. That was the policy pursued at the time. As for the service itself, I already explained how it operated at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, you misunderstand. Your later appointment to the chief of the CSB Doboj once the CSB Doboj was part and parcel of what was then known as the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as my status was concerned, there was continuity. I'm not quite sure if I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It may be my fault and I accept that entirely. It would not be right, would it, to suggest that your appointment as chief of the CSB Doboj when it was part of the Republika Srpska had anything to do with the SAO Northern Bosnia or Mr. Perisic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. The centre operated, as you saw, until the end of April and the reports and everything else was being sent to the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You see, when this was happening and I don't see any connection between the two.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You never became a member of any Crisis Staff of the SAO Northern Bosnia because no such thing existed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't a member of any Crisis Staff, neither of those in existence nor any other that didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you did not take orders, did you, from Mr. Perisic or instructions from Mr. Perisic or from your cousin, Mr. Bjelosevic, in their capacities as president or vice-president of the SAO Northern Bosnia Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I would like to reiterate once again as far as I can remember these things were not functioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Whether they functioned properly or not, officially, Mr. Perisic, apart from being the head of the Municipal Assembly in Teslic -- or Serbian Municipal Assembly in Teslic, also held officially the title of president of the Assembly of the Serb autonomous region of Northern Bosnia, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what the decision reads. However, these are political issues that I don't know much about, therefore I don't believe I am capable of giving you proper answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but this declaration whether or not in reality it ever worked or not of the Serb autonomous region of Northern Bosnia was part and parcel, wasn't it, of the planned break-up of Bosnia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it all depends on the angle from which you perceive things. One may look at it that way, but, on the other hand, one may look at it from the point of view of the ambition to preserve Yugoslavia and prevent the cessation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Again, I say these are political issues and probably would warrant some more sensitive analysis because this is really not an area of my expertise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you see, Mr. Bjelosevic, I understand that you are saying you are a policeman. But I thought we had already established, politics and the police, however regrettably, were inextricably mixed up, weren't they, certainly by November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw from some documents that the policy pursued by all political parties was based on their wish to exert as much influence as they could. As I understand things, people want to gain power in order to exert influence, and I can only speak relevantly about the issue that pertained to the Doboj CSB, given the fact that my reaction to every political pressure was as we discussed here already.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand what you are saying was your reaction, but my question was a very simple one: Do you agree, it can be answered yes or no, that by -- certainly by November 1991, politics and the MUP were mixed up together?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was influence, however I don't think we can say that things were mixed up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Let's just move on a few days, shall we. The next document, please, is P2095, tab 7D. Now, this is the document that was issued by -- adopted by the Assembly of the Serbian people on the 21st of November as a result of the plebiscite which took place on the 9th and 10th of November. Did you vote in that plebiscite, Mr. Bjelosevic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you vote in favour?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In favour of Yugoslavia, yes, I did, and even nowadays if I could do anything to bring this state back, I would do my best to achieve that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You see, it says: "The decision on the territories, municipalities, local communes, and inhabited places, Bosnia-Herzegovina, are considered as territory of the federal state of Yugoslavia. The territories of municipalities, local communes, and inhabited places, where on the 9th and 10th of November, the plebiscite was conducted for the Serbian people and other peoples to opt for remaining in the common state of Yugoslavia together with the Republic of Serbia, Montenegro, the Serbian Autonomous District region of Krajina." That refers not to north-west Krajina and Bosnia but to the area in Croatia, does it not? Mr. Bjelosevic, the Krajina there is not the Bosnian Krajina but what loosely, I will call, the Croatia Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me a minute just to look at it more closely, which paragraph in particular was that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Under 1.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is a whole list here of what is to be incorporated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't want anybody to be confused. The Krajina mentioned here is not the Serb Autonomous Region of Krajina in north-west Bosnia where Zupljanin was head of the CSB, it is the Krajina over the border in Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please assist me to find this particular portion. I really went through all the paragraphs. Is it immediately under where it says the decision under Roman numeral I?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but, please, I think it's self-evident anyhow, so I'm not going to trouble you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry. I'm probably missing what you are suggesting, Ms. Korner. This is precisely the region Krajina from Bosnia-Herzegovina. It says: "The decision on verification of the proclaimed Serbian autonomous district in Bosnia-Herzegovina." And all the municipalities are actually Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... no, if you look -- unless we have a translation problem. The plebiscite was conducted for the Serbian people and other peoples to opt for remaining in the common state of Yugoslavia together with the Republic of Serbia, the Republic of Montenegro, the SAO of Krajina, the SAO Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Now, as far as I know, Montenegro is not in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. But you are directing us to under I and it says "Autonomous Region of Krajina." I don't have the document, unfortunately, with me and I don't know where you are reading from.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And I should maybe suggest that you provide the copy of the whole document for the benefit of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I was looking at my own copy and it's the wrong document that was up. I apologise, I wasn't looking at the document on the screen and I don't know -- sorry. It should be, I thought as I said, P20 -- it's a different document. Your Honour, it's my fault. I think I've got it. There's a different document which has gone in as a document from the one I'm looking at. But it doesn't really matter because I just wanted to know whether Mr. Bjelosevic had voted in the plebiscite.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, one other question: After the plebiscite in February was held the referendum, that's right, isn't it, February 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 29th of February, and I think on the 1st of March as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I just want to ask you to look at one further document on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's P1936. Tab 8B.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is slightly jumping ahead, but at its session held on the 26th of January, 1992, the Assembly of the republic adopted the following: The decision to hold a referendum for the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina which would be a basis for transforming Bosnia and Herzegovina into an independent state, was adopted in a regular manner and without presence of the Serbian deputies. Can only be binding on these two peoples. For the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, this decision is invalid and directed against the existential interests. Mr. Krajisnik, as president of the Assembly, was making the point, wasn't he, that nobody should vote, no Serbs should vote in this referendum; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is another political decision and political affairs. In order for you to understand me and my attitude towards certain political issues, let me tell you just one thing: There was a political rift back in 1997 in Republika Srpska, and this rift spread around. We had Biljana Plavsic as the president on the one side, and the government, headed by Mr. Klicko [phoen], on the other side. No, no, please let me explain my position. I didn't want to take sides at that time either. That was my principle. I always thought that the political issues should never be tackled by either the army or the police, otherwise that could be called a coup d'etat and it could produce completely different consequences. I didn't want to be part of that. I can read this document and tell you what I think about it, but I, myself, was never directly involved in this. And I always advocated a position that nobody from the police should be involved in that, either at that time or in 1997, so I have subscribed to the same position and attitude throughout the whole period. I have never been involved in politics and I always stayed away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you don't consider the fact that you voted in the plebiscite in November was making a political decision or taking a political standpoint?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my personal attitude which was conditioned on anything -- wasn't conditioned on anything else. It wasn't imposed on me by anyone. That was my constitutional right. And I would like to say once again, I still believe that the greatest mistake that was made was that Yugoslavia was broken up and that it ended in a war. That used to be quite comfortable and good country for everyone living in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you exercise your personal vote and decision in the referendum and vote against the independence of Bosnia so that, as you put it, Yugoslavia could be kept together?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already stated my preferences when it was a for-or-against Yugoslavia. Of course I couldn't vote once for and the second time vote against -- if you can help me, if I misunderstood your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You did. You told us you took part in the Serb plebiscite held in November. You exercised your personal right to vote, nothing to do with politics, so that in favour of Bosnia staying in Yugoslavia. Did you equally exercise that vote, your right to vote when the referendum was held, and vote against the suggestion that Bosnia should be independent but instead vote again for staying in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go to the referendum for the second time because I had already voted once before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, you are not telling the Court, are you, that you didn't realise that this was something completely separate. If you were so keen on Bosnia staying in Yugoslavia and you did not consider that politics was something that should concern you, why didn't you vote in the referendum?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because the referendum was aimed at getting Bosnia-Herzegovina out of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But if you had voted against it and enough Serbs had gone along and voted against it, things might have been different, mightn't they?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was my understanding that the outcome was the same because not voting and voting against boiled down to the same thing. Voting in favour meant voting to have Bosnia and Herzegovina taken out of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, you know exactly what I mean and I'm going to pursue this, Mr. Bjelosevic. By that time, by the time the referendum was held at the end of February, it was absolutely plain to you, wasn't it, that there was going to be an independent state -- Serbian state within Bosnia? That had already been declared, hadn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not clear to me, and I don't think that it was clear to anyone at the time what would happen next. If you remember, there was lively diplomatic and political activity underway at the time, both in the area of Yugoslavia and also with mediators in Geneva, and I cannot remember now who were all the people involved in unravelling this crisis. I think that in that period of time February, March, no one was clear on what would happen, at least it wasn't clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Just have a look, please, at the document which is apparently part of the law library, L00029 exhibit, tab 8A. On the 9th of January, 1992, the Assembly of the Serbian people declared the Republic of the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, you are not telling the Court, are you, Mr. Bjelosevic, that you didn't know that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Bjelosevic, you have to start again, the interpreters didn't hear you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I wonder whether the usher could see whether his microphones need to be adjusted because this appears to be a recurring problem.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can hear speakers when all other microphones are switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it all right now?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it seems that although this is not a problem that's occurred in the early years that if anybody else leaves a microphone on, the interpreters cannot hear the witness. I don't know why that is and it shouldn't be. There's something obviously wrong with the sound system, but it meant, I gather from what the interpreters are saying, that's the problem. I am afraid I am the guilty one because I forget to turn it off when I ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We are observing that your microphone seems to be more sensitive than any of the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I could try using the other microphone, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Bjelosevic, I was asking you whether you were aware of the declaration of proclaiming the Serbian Republic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was publicly declared. It was a generally known thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the first part, it says: "In the area of the Serbian autonomous regions and districts and other Serbian entities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, including the areas where the Serbian people are a minority due to genocide committed against them during the Second World War, and on the basis of the plebiscite, the republic of the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina is hereby established and proclaimed." What do you understand -- no, that would invite a very long answer. So let me put this to you: Where the areas where the Serbian people are in a minority due to genocide, that meant areas which were -- had a majority of non-Serbs, did it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which area this referred to. I really would not take it upon myself to interpret what this means.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, there were a number of municipalities, weren't there, which later on were claimed to be part of the Serbian Republic where the Serbs were not in a majority?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the territories were being declared at the time and there were inter-party talks that were being held so such and such Serb municipality was declared, such and such Croatian municipality. And Crisis Staffs were later formed on the basis of that principle, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not an answer to my question and you know it's not. There were municipalities which were claimed to be part of the Serb Republic, were there not, where the Serbs were not actually the majority population?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can speak for the area where I worked. As far as I know, in all these areas, in all these municipalities, some kind of inter-party agreements had been reached and this was divided. It wasn't that an entire municipality would be taken as such. Say the Serb municipality of Derventa would be proclaimed or Teslic, and as you could see, there was Doboj Istok, et cetera, some kind of inter-party agreements were reached there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, your municipality is one, we'll look in more detail at Doboj, but there were according to the census in 1991, 39 -- nearly 40.000 Serbs, 41.000 Muslims, and 13.000 Croats. So that's an area where the Serbs were not a majority; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I don't know whether you know specifically that some lines and divisions were agreed upon between the SDA, the SDS and the HDZ, and the result of that was the existence of these municipalities that we've already discussed, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am a going to -- yes, no, no, no, you say, Mr. Bjelosevic -- I'm going to come back in detail to Doboj, but I just want to deal with this declaration which said that where Serbs were in a minority due to genocide. Let's take Prijedor, for example, there were 49.000 Muslims, 47.000 Serbs and 8.000 Croats. So, again, Prijedor, that was not a municipality, was it, where the Serbs had a majority?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the information you have presented now is accurate, and I'm not doubting it at all, there's nothing I can say to that. I was not in Prijedor. I'm not familiar with all these details, but then that's the way it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But you are an intelligent man, Mr. Bjelosevic, and you know full well the point I'm making. The moment that there was this declaration of the Serb -- so-called Serb Republic on the so-called Serb Assembly in January 1992, it was inevitable, was it not, that there would be conflict?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't inevitable still, although preparations for war were underway and formations were being established but it wasn't inevitable to have them used.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You see, I've just been through this, I am afraid, at some length because it's all a background, isn't it, to the meeting of the 11th of February, 1992, attended by you and other high-ranking Serb MUP officials. And it's right, isn't it, Mr. Bjelosevic, that when you and all of you attended, you all knew there was going to be a split in the MUP, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that no one could have said that with any certainty. After all, you saw from the minutes what I was saying, and I think that that was still an attempt to bring pressure to bear against the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to have it function in a lawful way, to do away with some unlawful things, and so on. I don't know how many times I have to repeat that we were denied proper supplies as we should have had on the basis of the regular programme of equipping the service. And I don't know how many times I have to repeat that in that period there was a parallel system that was established. You saw through those inspectors who came to the area and they established a parallel system of management. Perhaps it was clear to some that there would be divisions, but it wasn't to me, believe me. To the very end, I harboured hopes to the effect that this would start functioning properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm going to come on to your action after [indiscernible] MUP later on, but I want to deal at this stage, please, with the events of the 11th of February. You have told the Court, as you say, endlessly about your string of complaints that a parallel system was being set up, that you weren't getting supplies, that people were being appointed who shouldn't have been appointed, and so on and so forth. Now, we've already looked at the first letter you ever wrote to the Mr. Delimustafic about those complaints in October. How did you get -- how did you come to attend the meeting on the 11th of February in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was invited to the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now I could not remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Look, you know full well, don't you, Mr. Bjelosevic, this was one of the most important meetings that took place. You've got perfect recollection of other important meetings. Are you seriously telling this Court you do not know who asked you to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know who invited me to the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was it Mr. Mandic whose phone number you had in your book?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that it was Mr. Mandic, but it was only natural that I would have the telephone number of the assistant minister for the area of crime prevention. It was quite proper for me to have the numbers of these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not could it, was it, in fact, Mr. Mandic who telephoned you or wrote to you and said, Attend this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you that I really do not remember who it was that called me. It may seem real or unreal to you, but I do not want to say anything that I do not know with certainty. I don't know who called me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was it made clear to you by whoever called you that this was a meeting of high-ranking Serbian members of the Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't even know the details what I was told at that point in time, but I know who attended the meeting and what was discussed there. And, after all, there are minutes about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Was it made clear to you that this was going to be a meeting of Serbian members of the MUP only?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember that that is what the information said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you understand, and was this supposed to be some sort of collegium? I mean, somebody must have told you what this meeting was about, otherwise why would you have gone?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the details, how I received this information and from whom and what that information said. I really do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that true, Mr. Bjelosevic, or is it just that you don't want to tell the Court that you knew this meeting was about the formation of a separate MUP?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I not want to say what I know?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the day before you went to the meeting in Banja Luka you attended another meeting, didn't you, which you recorded in your diary?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
